title: Gauda Kingdom
capsule: The Gauda Kingdom was a short-lived but historically significant polity in the Bengal delta region of northeastern India, ruled by Shashanka (r. c. 590–625 CE), the first historically prominent independent king of Bengal, who governed from his capital at Karnasuvarna near modern Murshidabad. Shashanka, a Shaivite Hindu who bore the title Maharajadhiraja, carved out a kingdom encompassing much of Bengal, Odisha, and Bihar and is recorded in Buddhist sources as a persecutor of Buddhist sites, reportedly destroying the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya. Following his death around 625 CE, his son Manava ruled briefly before Gauda fragmented, and Bengal entered the anarchic period described in sources as Matsyanyaya ("law of fish") until the Pala dynasty's rise around 750 CE gave the region its next stable kingdom.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The extent of the Gauda Kingdom is attested primarily from the Harshacharita of Bana and the accounts of Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang; precise territorial limits are inferred from these literary sources and are not archaeologically defined.
